topic: Introduction and History of Aviation Insurance
t: Tata Airlines, India's first commercial airline, was renamed and became a public company in 1946 under the name:
e: Tata Airlines became Air India Ltd in 1946; Air India International was formed in 1948 for overseas routes before nationalisation in 1953.

t: The so-called 'critical eleven minutes' of a flight refers to:
o: The first eleven minutes of cruise
The time allowed for an emergency evacuation
Roughly three minutes of take-off/climb and eight minutes of approach/landing, when most accidents occur
e: These phases close to the ground carry the greatest accident exposure, which is why underwriters look closely at the number of take-offs and landings (cycles) and not just hours flown.

t: A 'code-share' arrangement between two airlines means that:
o: The two airlines merge their fleets
Both airlines use the same aircraft registration
One airline sells seats under its own flight code on a flight operated by the other airline
Pilots are exchanged between the airlines
e: Code-sharing creates the contracting carrier/actual carrier situation addressed by the Guadalajara Convention and Montreal 1999 Chapter V, affecting which carrier and insurer faces passenger claims.

t: Which ICAO Annex sets the standards for Security – safeguarding international civil aviation against acts of unlawful interference?
e: Annex 17 is Security; Annex 6 is Operation of Aircraft, Annex 8 Airworthiness and Annex 13 Accident and Incident Investigation.

t: Operations into high-altitude mountain airstrips (for example in the Himalayan region) are rated more heavily by underwriters because of:
o: Reduced engine and wing performance in thin air, short or sloping runways and rapidly changing weather
e: Density altitude reduces lift and engine power, and such strips often lack navigation aids and go-around options, materially increasing accident risk.

topic: Aviation Insurance Market and Classification of Risks
t: Lloyd's of London is best described as:
o: A market where syndicates backed by members underwrite risks brought by Lloyd's brokers
e: Lloyd's is a marketplace; each syndicate underwrites for its own account, and aviation risks are placed through Lloyd's brokers on subscription.

topic: Aviation Insurance Market and Classification of Risks
t: GIC Re, the Indian national reinsurer that participates in Indian aviation programmes, was constituted as a reinsurer in:
e: GIC was reorganised as the national reinsurer in 2000 (effective from that year) when its four subsidiaries were delinked and the market opened to private insurers.

topic: Aviation Insurance Market and Classification of Risks
t: An aviation risk is placed 25% with an Indian insurer and the balance with four reinsurers. Lead reinsurer shares are 30%, with the other three taking 15% each. On a claim of ₹60 crore, the lead reinsurer pays:
e: Each participant pays its subscribed share: 30% of ₹60 crore = ₹18 crore. Subscription placements are several, not joint.

t: The Warsaw Convention 1929 originally limited an air carrier's liability for death or injury of a passenger to:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Warsaw 1929 fixed the limit at 125,000 gold francs; the Hague Protocol 1955 doubled it to 250,000 francs, and the Montreal Agreement 1966 raised it to US $75,000 for flights touching the USA.

topic: Aviation Insurance Market and Classification of Risks
t: Which of the following is classified as an 'aerial work' operation?
o: A flying club solo training flight
e: Aerial work covers specialised commercial uses such as photography, survey, crop spraying, fire-fighting and banner towing, each with its own hazard rating.

t: When a hull total loss is paid and the wreckage is subsequently sold by insurers for ₹8 crore on an agreed value of ₹100 crore, the net cost of the claim to insurers is:
e: Insurers pay the full agreed value of ₹100 crore to the insured and recover ₹8 crore from salvage, a net cost of ₹92 crore; salvage is not deducted from the insured's payment.

t: The 'Ground' risk under a hull policy refers to the aircraft:
o: While stationary or being moved otherwise than under its own power (e.g. towed or parked)
e: Ground risks (hangar fire, hail, towing damage, vehicle impact) are rated lowest; taxiing and flight carry progressively higher rates.

t: A lessor requires the aircraft to be insured for an agreed value of ₹400 crore, though the airline estimates market value at ₹320 crore. The airline insures at ₹400 crore. On a total loss, insurers pay:
e: Under an agreed value policy the agreed figure is paid; underwriters accepted the lease-required value at inception, usually within an allowed margin over market value.

t: Under the hull section of AVN 1C, if insurers elect to pay for a total loss they are entitled to:
o: Deduct the deductible and the salvage
Retain the premium for the next year
Take over the aircraft (salvage) and all the insured's rights in it
e: Payment of the amount insured on a total loss transfers the salvage to insurers; the deductible does not apply to a total loss.

t: Which of the following statements regarding hull cover for an aircraft engine removed from the airframe for overhaul is correct?
o: It is normally covered under a separate Spares policy, unless the hull policy is specifically extended
It remains covered under the hull policy while in the workshop
It is covered under the pilot's PA policy
e: Hull cover attaches to the aircraft as a unit; detached engines and parts require spares all risks cover for storage, transit and workshop risks.

t: A hull policy's 'other insurance' or 'sole indemnity' condition provides that:
o: The insured may recover the same loss under two policies
The policy is void if any other insurance exists
Insurers will not pay for loss recoverable under any other policy except for any excess beyond that policy, so the insured cannot profit from double insurance
e: The condition applies the principle of indemnity and contribution; it does not void cover but prevents double recovery.

t: Under the Montreal Convention 1999, a passenger's claim for damage caused by delay is limited (as originally adopted) to:
e: Article 22(1) fixed delay liability at 4,150 SDR per passenger (revised upward since); 1,000 SDR was the baggage limit and 17 SDR/kg the cargo limit.

t: Under Article 21 of the Montreal Convention, for a passenger claim exceeding the first tier, the carrier escapes liability for the excess if it proves that:
o: The passenger was not wearing a seat belt
The damage was not due to the negligence or wrongful act of the carrier or its servants, or was solely due to a third party
e: The second tier reverses the burden of proof onto the carrier; insurers therefore usually reserve rather than contest claims above the first tier.

t: The first-tier limit under Montreal 1999 from 28 December 2019 is 128,821 SDR. If 1 SDR = ₹110, the rupee equivalent per passenger (approximately) is:
e: 128,821 × ₹110 = ₹1,41,70,310, i.e. about ₹1.42 crore of strict liability per passenger before the carrier can raise any defence.

t: AVN 1C Section IV 'General Exclusions' applies to:
o: Sections I, II and III of the policy
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). The general exclusions (illegal use, outside geographical limits, unnamed pilots, unairworthy condition, war, noise, nuclear, etc.) apply across all three operative sections.

t: The third-party liability of an aircraft operator under EU Regulation 785/2004 and under the Rome Convention 1952 is graded according to:
o: The maximum take-off mass (weight) of the aircraft
e: Surface damage potential rises with aircraft weight, so minimum third-party limits are set in bands by MTOM.

t: Which of the following is correct about Section III (passenger liability) of AVN 1C?
o: It covers the insured's crew as passengers
It covers bodily injury to passengers and loss of or damage to their baggage and personal articles while on board, boarding or disembarking
It covers liability for delay only
e: Section III indemnifies legal liability to passengers for injury and baggage; crew are excluded as employees and cargo requires separate extension.

t: Under LSW 555D and AVN 52E, insurers may, by giving 7 days' notice, review and amend:
o: The agreed value of the aircraft
The premium and/or the geographical limits for war cover
e: War cover is volatile; insurers reserve the right on 7 days' notice to revise premium and geographical limits (e.g. excluding a territory where conflict has broken out).

t: AVN 52E typically provides third-party war liability cover subject to:
o: A sub-limit any one occurrence and in the annual aggregate, lower than the main policy CSL
e: After 2001 markets imposed sub-limits for third-party (non-passenger) war liability; passenger war liability is usually written back to the full policy limit.

t: Paragraph (d) of AVN 48B excludes loss arising from:
o: Any act of one or more persons, whether or not agents of a sovereign power, for political or terrorist purposes
e: Paragraph (d) is the political/terrorist act exclusion; confiscation is (f) and nuclear detonation (b).

t: Which of the following is NOT one of the five operative/structural sections of the AVN 1C London Aircraft Insurance Policy?
o: Section I – Loss of or damage to aircraft
Section III – Legal liability to passengers
Section IV – General exclusions applicable to all sections
e: AVN 1C has Sections I (hull), II (third party), III (passengers), IV (general exclusions) and V (conditions); loss of licence is a separate policy.

t: An aviation hull policy with annual premium ₹1.46 crore provides a lay-up return of 50% of the pro-rata premium for any continuous lay-up of 30 days or more. An aircraft is laid up for 90 days with no claims. The return premium is:
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Pro-rata premium for 90 days = ₹1.46 crore × 90/365 = ₹36 lakh; 50% of this = ₹18 lakh is returned.

t: The cancellation condition in an aircraft hull and liability policy normally provides that:
o: Either party may cancel on giving the stipulated notice, with pro-rata (insured) or short-period return of premium as specified
e: Standard conditions allow cancellation by notice; where AVN 67B applies, contract parties must also receive their 30-day notice.

t: A Loss of Licence policy with sum insured ₹1 crore pays a temporary benefit of 1% of the sum insured per month after a waiting period of 3 months, for a maximum of 24 months. A pilot is medically grounded for 9 months and then regains his licence. The benefit paid is:
e: Benefit runs for 9 − 3 = 6 months at ₹1 lakh per month = ₹6 lakh.

t: The products liability section of an airport operator's policy would respond to a claim arising from:
o: Contaminated aviation fuel sold by the airport causing an aircraft engine failure
A passenger tripping on a staircase
A hangar roof collapsing on a customer's aircraft
An airport vehicle striking a parked aircraft
e: Fuel and other goods supplied are products; the staircase is premises liability and the hangar collapse is hangarkeepers' liability.

t: A corporate owner wants cover for the hull of its jet against war and terrorism risks. This is obtained by:
o: Purchasing a separate hull war policy (LSW 555D) or endorsing the hull policy with a war write-back
Deleting AVN 48B from the hull policy
Buying a loss of licence policy
Relying on AVN 52E, which covers hulls
e: AVN 52E only writes back liability; hull war requires LSW 555D or equivalent, often placed with a separate specialist war market.

t: Which of the following best describes 'loss of use' or 'business interruption' cover for aircraft?
o: It is a separate cover, rarely purchased, paying a daily indemnity while the aircraft is out of service after insured damage
It is included automatically in every hull policy
It is another name for lay-up return
It covers loss of the pilot's employment
e: Hull policies exclude loss of use; a separate policy with a daily limit and waiting period may be bought, but it is uncommon.

t: An airline wishes to cover its liability for cargo and mail carried. Under a standard AVN 1C policy this liability is:
o: Not covered unless specifically extended by endorsement for cargo legal liability
Covered under the hull war policy
e: AVN 1C covers passengers and third parties; cargo and mail legal liability (subject to convention limits) is added by endorsement at additional premium.

t: An airline's passenger liability premium is adjustable at ₹10 per passenger carried. A deposit premium is charged on an estimate of 50 lakh passengers. Actual passengers carried are 60 lakh. The adjustment premium payable at year-end is:
e: Deposit = ₹5 crore (50 lakh × ₹10); actual = ₹6 crore; additional premium of ₹1 crore is due on adjustment.

t: 'Burning cost' as used by reinsurers in rating an aviation excess of loss layer is:
o: The historical losses that would have fallen into the layer, expressed as a percentage of the cedant's premium income, used to price the layer
The cost of fire damage to aircraft
e: Burning cost rating applies past experience to the layer; it is loaded for expenses, IBNR and profit to produce the XL rate.

t: Third-party insurance is compulsory for a motor vehicle used in a public place under which section of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988?
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 146 makes TP cover compulsory; Section 164 fixes no-fault compensation (₹5 lakh death / ₹2.5 lakh grievous hurt).

t: Which of the following statements about hull deductibles for airlines is correct?
o: Deductibles are the same for all aircraft types regardless of size
Deductibles apply to total losses only
Larger jet aircraft usually carry higher deductibles, often expressed in US dollars, and may have separate ingestion deductibles
e: Deductibles scale with aircraft size and value, and ingestion deductibles are set per engine to keep frequent FOD claims out of the all-risks policy.

t: Under the Warsaw Convention as amended by the Hague Protocol, a passenger killed on an international flight between two Hague states gives rise to a limited claim of (before any wilful misconduct finding):
e: The Hague Protocol doubled the Warsaw limit to 250,000 Poincaré francs; Montreal 1999 replaced this with the two-tier SDR system where it applies.

t: Montreal Protocol No. 4 of 1975 is important because it:
o: Modernised the cargo provisions of Warsaw, allowing electronic documentation and SDR limits
e: Protocol No. 4 replaced the cargo documentation rules and introduced the 17 SDR/kg cargo limit with strict liability, later carried into Montreal 1999.

t: Under Article 17 of the Warsaw/Montreal regime, the carrier is liable for passenger injury caused by an 'accident' on board or while embarking/disembarking. In Air France v. Saks (1985) the US Supreme Court held that an 'accident' is:
o: Only a crash of the aircraft
An unexpected or unusual event or happening external to the passenger, not the passenger's own internal reaction to normal operations
e: A passenger's hearing loss from normal cabin pressurisation was not an 'accident'; the event must be unusual and external to the passenger.

t: The Guatemala City Protocol 1971 proposed to amend the Warsaw Convention by introducing strict carrier liability for passengers with an unbreakable limit. Its status is that it:
o: Was replaced by the Chicago Convention
Never came into force for lack of sufficient ratifications
e: Guatemala City required ratification by states accounting for a large share of traffic (including the USA) and never entered into force; Montreal 1999 achieved its aims differently.

t: The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) has its headquarters in:
e: ICAO, a specialised agency of the UN created by the Chicago Convention, is headquartered in Montreal, Canada, which is also where IATA is based.

t: Since 1 April 2021, the standard fire policy for a dwelling in India is:
o: Standard Fire and Special Perils Policy
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Bharat Griha Raksha for homes; Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha (up to ₹5 crore) and Bharat Laghu Udyam Suraksha (₹5–50 crore) for enterprises.

t: The rules under which the AAIB investigates accidents in India are the:
o: Aircraft (Investigation of Accidents and Incidents) Rules 2017
e: The 2017 Rules (replacing the 2012 Rules) implement Annex 13 in India and define accident, serious incident and incident for investigation purposes.

t: Under ICAO Annex 13, an 'incident' is:
o: An occurrence, other than an accident, associated with the operation of an aircraft which affects or could affect the safety of operation
e: Incidents are safety-related occurrences falling short of accidents; serious incidents are those where an accident nearly occurred.

t: An aircraft is destroyed on the ground by an explosion whose cause (accidental fuel vapour ignition or a sabotage device) cannot be immediately determined. The agreed value is ₹300 crore. Under AVS 103, the hull all-risks and hull war insurers each pay provisionally:
e: The 50/50 clause requires each market to advance half (₹150 crore) so the insured is paid promptly; the final allocation follows determination of the cause.

t: Which of the following statements about the handling of passenger death claims after an airline accident is INCORRECT?
o: Insurers normally appoint lawyers and adjusters in the relevant jurisdictions
Claims are settled under the liability regime applicable to the particular carriage (Warsaw, Hague or Montreal)
Advance payments to families are commonly made without admission of liability
The airline may freely admit liability and settle claims without insurer consent
e: The policy conditions prohibit admissions or settlements without insurers' consent; everything else described is normal practice.

t: An aviation XL layer of ₹50 crore excess of ₹10 crore has an annual premium of ₹5 crore with one reinstatement at pro-rata additional premium. A loss uses ₹20 crore of the layer. The reinstatement premium payable is:
e: Pro-rata reinstatement: (20/50) × ₹5 crore = ₹2 crore, restoring the full ₹50 crore limit for further losses.

t: A 'stop loss' reinsurance treaty protects an aviation insurer against:
o: Any single loss above a fixed amount
Its aggregate annual loss ratio exceeding an agreed percentage of premium
e: Stop loss responds when total losses for the year exceed a stated loss ratio, protecting overall results rather than individual risks or events.

t: A 'claims control clause' (as opposed to claims co-operation) in a facultative aviation reinsurance gives the reinsurer:
o: The right to control the investigation, negotiation and settlement of claims, the cedant being bound to follow its instructions
The duty to pay claims directly to the insured
The right to cancel the policy after a claim
e: Where a fronting insurer retains little or nothing, reinsurers usually insist on claims control; claims co-operation requires only notification and consultation.
